title: At 50, Your Brain Starts Replacing its Own Immune Cells
description: Team, A study came out in Science this month that I’d put among the most important things published on brain aging this year, and I’ve barely seen anyone talk about it. They collected 40 human brains from people who had died between their twenties and their nineties. The group was built on purpose: men and women, spread evenly across four age brackets from 20 to 100, so no stretch of life was over-represented. Then they went into the hippocampus, your memory center and the first region Alzheimer’s takes apart, and they read the cells one at a time. Most brain studies can’t do that. They grind up tissue and measure the average across millions of cells at once, which blurs young in with old and healthy in with failing. This team read individual cells, about 295,000 of them. And in each one they didn’t just record which genes were switched on. They used two techniques across the same brains. The first read, cell by cell, which genes were active and which stretches of DNA were physically open versus locked shut. The second read the chemical marks sitting on the DNA and the way the DNA was folded in three dimensions inside the nucleus. Four layers of information where most studies get one, sorted into 18 different cell types, tracked across a whole human lifespan. For this part of the brain, that had not really been done before. How do you calm down your nervous system? This newsletter is about the two systems that age your hippocampus: inflammation and energy. The daily levers I named for those were your sleep, your muscle, your blood sugar, and your stress load. That last one is where this fits.

title: Men AND Women Need Estrogen.
description: Team, A friend of mine, forty-six, sharp as a blade, sat in a doctor’s office last month and asked a simple question. Should she start hormone therapy, for her brain. She got a shrug. Some vague reassurance. A line about how the evidence is mixed. She left with nothing, which is what most women leave with, and she called me frustrated, because she’s not asking out of vanity. Her mother has Alzheimer’s. She’s watching the clock. Here’s what nobody put in front of her, and it’s the thing I want to put in front of you. The reason she couldn’t get a clean answer is not that the science is thin. It’s that the real science is inconvenient . It doesn’t fit on a prescription pad or in a headline, and so it gets flattened into “the evidence is mixed,” which is true and also useless. You already know the hormone-therapy wars. You know the WHI, the backlash, the slow rehabilitation. I’m not going to relitigate 2002 with you. You’re smarter than that conversation. I want to take you underneath it, to the part that actually decides the answer. Start here, because this is the sentence that reorganized how I think about the female brain. In a landmark review, Roberta Brinton and her colleagues argue that perimenopause is not a reproductive event at all. It’s a neurological one. And estrogen, they write, is not a sex hormone that happens to visit the brain. It is a master regulator of how the brain makes and spends energy (Brinton et al., Nature Reviews Endocrinology, 2015). Sit with that word. Master regulator. Of energy. In the most energy-hungry organ you own. Just moment to celebrate me finally meeting Dr Rhonda Patrick. We both spoke last week in Vancouver. The organ that runs hot Your brain is a furnace.

title: Vox Media Should Be Ashamed of This Headline
description: I saw a headline this week that made me genuinely angry, and I don’t say that lightly. It was one of those big, hopeful, a-corner-has-been-turned Alzheimer’s headlines. The kind that a woman whose mother is slipping away reads on her phone at midnight and feels her chest unclench for a second. The kind that makes a family think, maybe. Maybe there’s something now. So I paid the two dollars and I read the whole thing. And here’s the strange part. The article itself is more careful than the headline. The reporter quotes the risks. He even notes that hype has outpaced the science before. But almost nobody reads the whole article. They read the headline, they feel the glow of it, and they walk away believing we are closer to a cure than we are. That gap, between what a skimmed headline implies and what the science actually says, is the thing that hurts real people. So let me walk you through what the science actually says. The story is really about two drugs. Lecanemab and donanemab. You may have seen the brand names, Leqembi and Kisunla. They are, to be fair, real progress, and I won’t take that from them. They are the first drugs that have clearly, definitively slowed the cognitive decline of Alzheimer’s in large trials. For a disease that has humiliated every treatment thrown at it for decades, that matters. But here is what the headline does not tell you, and what every family deserves to know before their hope gets hijacked. These drugs do not make anyone better. Let me be precise, because precision is the whole point here. In the trials, lecanemab slowed decline by about 27% and donanemab by around 35% over eighteen months (van Dyck et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2023; Sims et al., JAMA, 2023). Read those numbers carefully.
